body.statement:
For every fixed \(K\) and \(c\in\mathcal C_K\), there is a sequence of permutation-invariant priors \(\Pi_n\) on the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{n\times K}\), chosen without reference to the assignment law, such that
\[
\inf_{r:\,\sum_ar_a=n}\operatorname{BR}_{\Pi_n}(r)
\ge n^{-1}-\Lambda_cn^{-4/3}-o(n^{-4/3}).
\]
The remainder is uniform over all count vectors, including allocation to inactive arms and every face on which one or more active arms have zero count.  Conditional on every fixed labeled assignment, the posterior regression is the exact regression of the random finite-population target \(\tau_c(y)\); the inequality remains valid after averaging under every possibly dependent outcome-independent design \(\mathcal D_n\) and against every randomized full-label estimator \(\widehat\tau\).
body.proof_tex:
Write \(d=|S_c|\) and, after relabeling active arms if necessary, choose an active coordinate \(a_0\).  For the transverse basis take
\[
d_j=e_{a_j}-\frac{c_{a_j}}{c_{a_0}}e_{a_0},\qquad j=1,\ldots,d-1.
\]
Then \(c^\top d_j=0\), the \(d_j\)'s span \(\ker(c^\top)\), and \(B=[v,d_1,\ldots,d_{d-1}]\) is invertible: applying \(c^\top\) to a null linear combination first kills its coefficient of \(v\), after which linear independence in the kernel kills all remaining coefficients.  Its first inverse row is \(c^\top\).

We first construct a proper response tube.  The identities
\[
e_a=b_{e_a}+b_{\mathbf1},\qquad -e_a=b_{\mathbf1-e_a}+b_{\mathbf0}
\]
give a finite nonnegative response-type representation of every vector.  Choose an optimal representation \(\lambda^{v,+}\) of \(v\), and choose any such representation \(\lambda^{j,+}\) of each \(d_j\).  Complementing response types gives representations \(\lambda^{v,-}\) and \(\lambda^{j,-}\) of the negative directions, with the same total masses and costs.  Denote the common total masses by \(L_v,L_j\), and the costs by
\[
k_v=\sum_t\lambda_t^{v,+}\theta_t^2=\kappa(c),
\qquad k_j=\sum_t\lambda_t^{j,+}\theta_t^2.
\]
Let \(p^0\) put mass \(1/2\) on each of the all-zero and all-one response types.  Fix \(T<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).  With \(\alpha=n^{-1/3}\), \(x\in[-T,T]\), and \(h_j\in[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\), define
\[
\begin{split}
p_t(x,h)=p_t^0+\alpha\bigg[&|x|\lambda_t^{v,\operatorname{sgn}(x)}
+\sum_j|h_j|\lambda_t^{j,\operatorname{sgn}(h_j)}\\
&-\left(L_v|x|+\sum_jL_j|h_j|\right)p_t^0\bigg].
\end{split}
\tag{10}
\]
At a zero coordinate either sign gives the same zero contribution.  The bracket in (10) has total mass zero.  If
\[
\alpha\left(L_vT+\varepsilon\sum_jL_j\right)\le\frac12,
\tag{11}
\]
then noncentral probabilities are nonnegative and each central probability is at least \(1/4\).  Thus (10) is a probability vector.  If a response type drawn from it is denoted by \(t\), direct use of the representation identities gives, with \(\zeta=xv+\sum_jh_jd_j\),
\[
\mathbb E b_t=\alpha\zeta,\qquad
\mathbb E\theta_t=\alpha x,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_t)
=\alpha\left\{\kappa(c)|x|+\sum_jk_j|h_j|\right\}-\alpha^2x^2.
\tag{12}
\]

Let \(f\) be a compactly supported continuous piecewise-polynomial function, positive in the interior of its support and zero at its endpoints.  Put
\[
w(x)=\frac{f(x)^2}{\int f^2},\qquad
J_x=\int\frac{w'(x)^2}{w(x)}\,dx
=4\frac{\int f'(x)^2\,dx}{\int f(x)^2\,dx}.
\]
Compact truncation, endpoint tapering, and rational piecewise-polynomial interpolation in the weighted Sobolev norm show directly from the definition of \(C_A\) that, for every \(\epsilon>0\), \(f\) can be chosen with rational knots and coefficients so that
\[
J_x+\kappa(c)\mathbb E_w|x|\le\Lambda_c+\epsilon.
\tag{13}
\]
Indeed, scaling \(x\mapsto\kappa(c)^{1/3}x\) changes the unit-scale variational value to \(\Lambda_c\); truncation makes both omitted integrals small, a linear taper makes the boundary contribution small, and rational interpolation is dense on the resulting compact interval in both the \(L^2\) and derivative norms.  Normalization is by the displayed ratio, so rational coefficients do not require a rational square root.

Independently for each transverse coordinate use the density
\[
\rho_\varepsilon(h)=\frac{15}{16\varepsilon}\left(1-\frac{h^2}{\varepsilon^2}\right)^2
\mathbf1\{|h|\le\varepsilon\}.
\]
It vanishes quadratically at both endpoints and has Fisher information
\[
J_h=\int\frac{\rho_\varepsilon'(h)^2}{\rho_\varepsilon(h)}\,dh
=\frac{10}{\varepsilon^2}.
\tag{14}
\]
Draw \((x,h)\) from \(w\prod_j\rho_\varepsilon\); conditionally draw the \(n\) active response vectors independently from (10); and draw all inactive-arm outcomes as independent fair bits, independently of everything else.  After integrating out \((x,h)\), this is a prior \(\Pi_n\) on the finite set of fixed schedules.  It is permutation invariant and is chosen without reference to the assignment design.

We now prove the exact-target reduction for an arbitrary fixed labeled assignment.  Let \(q_a=r_a/n\) on active arms and \(Q=\sum_{a\in S_c}q_a\le1\).  Conditional on \((x,h)\), define
\[
\mu=\mathbb E\theta_t=\alpha x,\quad
\mu_a=\mathbb E b_{t,a},\quad
V_a=\operatorname{Var}(b_{t,a})=\frac14-\mu_a^2,\quad
C_a=\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_t,b_{t,a}),\quad
\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(\theta_t).
\]
There are finite tube-dependent constants \(L,\Gamma\) such that
\[
|\mu_a|\le\alpha L,\qquad |C_a|\le\alpha\Gamma.
\tag{15}
\]
The first bound follows from compactness of the parameter box.  For the second, \(\mathbb E_{p^0}(\theta_tb_{t,a})=0\), while (10) is affine on each of finitely many sign cells.  Hence a finite maximum of its coefficients supplies \(\Gamma\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\), \(4\alpha^2L^2\le1/2\), and thus
\[
\frac18\le V_a\le\frac14,\qquad
\frac1{V_a}\le4(1+u),\qquad u=8\alpha^2L^2.
\tag{16}
\]

The observed centered outcome on an active arm has only the two values \(\pm1/2\).  Therefore its conditional regression is exactly affine:
\[
\mathbb E(\theta_t\mid x,h,b_{t,a})
=\mu+\frac{C_a}{V_a}(b_{t,a}-\mu_a).
\]
If \(O\) denotes all labels and observed outcomes, independence across units gives the exact posterior-regression precursor
\[
m_{x,h}(O):=\mathbb E\{\tau_c(y)\mid x,h,O\}
=\mu+\frac1n\sum_{i:Z_i\in S_c}
\frac{C_{Z_i}}{V_{Z_i}}(b_{t_i,Z_i}-\mu_{Z_i}).
\tag{17}
\]
Inactive observations are absent from (17) because they were made ancillary.  Applying the conditional-variance identity first given \((x,h,O)\), and then given \(O\), yields the exact decomposition
\[
\operatorname{BR}_{\Pi_n}(r)
=\frac1n\mathbb E\left(\sigma^2-\sum_aq_a\frac{C_a^2}{V_a}\right)
+\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}\{m_{x,h}(O)\mid O\}.
\tag{18}
\]
This is a decomposition for the random finite-population target itself, not for its conditional mean \(\mu\).

We next derive the directional Bayes inequality used in every count regime.  Let \(D\) be a fixed directional derivative in the \((x,h)\) coordinates such that
\[
D\mu=\alpha,\qquad D\mu_a=\alpha z_a.
\]
Let \(S_D\) be the directional score of the joint parameter-observation density.  The endpoint-vanishing priors eliminate the outer boundary terms.  Formula (10), and hence (17), is continuous across every sign cell; its weak derivative is piecewise bounded, so the internal face terms cancel in pairs.  The same statement holds at spline knots by continuity.  Thus weak integration by parts is legitimate and gives
\[
\mathbb E\bigl[(m_{x,h}(O)-\mathbb E\{m_{x,h}(O)\mid O\})S_D\bigr]
=-\mathbb E(Dm_{x,h}(O)).
\tag{19}
\]
The derivative of \(C_a/V_a\) in (17) is multiplied by \(b_{t_i,a}-\mu_a\), whose conditional mean is zero.  The remaining terms give
\[
\mathbb E(Dm_{x,h}(O))
=\alpha\left[1-\sum_aq_a\mathbb E\left(\frac{z_aC_a}{V_a}\right)\right].
\tag{20}
\]
The conditional mean of the joint score given \(O\) is zero.  The prior and likelihood scores are orthogonal, distinct-unit likelihood scores are conditionally orthogonal, and a Bernoulli variable with mean \(1/2+\mu_a\) has information \((D\mu_a)^2/V_a\).  Consequently
\[
\mathbb E S_D^2=J_D+n\alpha^2\sum_aq_a\mathbb E(z_a^2/V_a).
\tag{21}
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz in (19)--(21) proves
\[
\mathbb E\operatorname{Var}\{m_{x,h}(O)\mid O\}
\ge
\frac{\alpha^2\left[1-\sum_aq_a\mathbb E(z_aC_a/V_a)\right]^2}
{J_D+n\alpha^2\sum_aq_a\mathbb E(z_a^2/V_a)}.
\tag{22}
\]
This derivation also proves that zero prior-density sets cause no omitted term: one first integrates on their complementary intervals and then takes limits, for which the quadratic endpoint zeros make the boundary products vanish.

We finish by treating all allocation strata uniformly.  Put \(\delta=n^{-1/8}\).  First suppose
\(\max_{a\in\mathcal A_K}|q_a-q_a^\star|\le\delta\), and use \(D=\partial_x\), so \(z=v\) and \(J_D=J_x\).  The exact covariance identity
\[
\sum_ac_aC_a=\operatorname{Cov}\left(\theta_t,\sum_ac_ab_{t,a}\right)=\sigma^2
\tag{23}
\]
and \(4q_a^\star v_a=c_a\) imply, using (15)--(16),
\[
\left|\sum_aq_a\mathbb E(v_aC_a/V_a)-\mathbb E\sigma^2\right|
\le4d\delta\alpha\Gamma+16\alpha^3\Gamma L^2.
\tag{24}
\]
Also \(\sum_aq_av_a^2/V_a\le1+u\) and
\(\sum_aq_aC_a^2/V_a\le4(1+u)\alpha^2\Gamma^2\).  Since
\[
\frac{(1-s)^2}{1+t}\ge1-2s-t\qquad(t\ge0),
\]
substitution in (18) and (22), followed by (12), gives
\[
\operatorname{BR}_{\Pi_n}(r)
\ge\frac1n-n^{-4/3}\left[J_x+\kappa(c)\mathbb E|x|
+\sum_jk_j\mathbb E|h_j|+e_{\mathrm{loc}}(n)\right],
\tag{25}
\]
where one valid explicit remainder is
\[
e_{\mathrm{loc}}(n)=8\alpha L^2+4(1+u)\alpha\Gamma^2
+8d\delta\Gamma+32\alpha^2\Gamma L^2=o(1).
\tag{26}
\]

Next suppose all active \(q_a\)'s are positive and the allocation is outside the preceding local set.  Define
\[
H=\sum_{a\in S_c}\frac{c_a^2}{q_a},\qquad
z_a=\frac{c_a}{q_aH},\qquad
\omega_a=\frac{c_a^2}{q_aH}.
\]
Then \(\omega_a\ge0\), \(\sum_a\omega_a=1\), and
\[
c^\top z=1,\qquad \sum_aq_az_a^2=H^{-1},\qquad
z=\sum_a\omega_a\frac{e_a}{c_a}.
\tag{27}
\]
Writing \(B^{-1}z=(1,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_{d-1})\), (27) shows
\[
|\beta_j|\le F_j:=\max_{a\in S_c}\left|\left(B^{-1}e_a/c_a\right)_{j+1}\right|.
\]
Thus the direction \(D_q=\partial_x+\sum_j\beta_j\partial_{h_j}\) has
\[
J_{D_q}=J_x+J_h\sum_j\beta_j^2\le J_{\max}:=J_x+J_h\sum_jF_j^2,
\tag{28}
\]
uniformly even as a positive allocation approaches a face.  By (23) and (27),
\[
\sum_aq_az_aC_a=\sigma^2/H.
\]
The bound \(|V_a^{-1}-4|\le32\alpha^2L^2\) therefore gives
\[
\left|\sum_aq_a\mathbb E(z_aC_a/V_a)-4\mathbb E\sigma^2/H\right|
\le64\alpha^3\Gamma L^2/H.
\tag{29}
\]
Furthermore, the normalization assumptions give the exact identity
\[
\Delta:=H-4
=4\sum_{a\in S_c}\frac{(q_a-q_a^\star)^2}{q_a}+4(1-Q).
\tag{30}
\]
If the local condition fails, (30) implies \(\Delta\ge\Delta_0:=4\delta^2\): an active deviation contributes at least \(4\delta^2\), while an inactive deviation gives \(1-Q>\delta\ge\delta^2\).

Let \(W=\kappa(c)T+\varepsilon\sum_jk_j\), \(j_n=\alpha J_{\max}\), and
\(D_0=4(1+u)+j_nH\).  From (12), \(0\le\sigma^2\le\alpha W\).  Multiplying (18) and (22) by \(nD_0\), using (16), (29), and dropping nonnegative squares yields, by direct expansion,
\[
\begin{split}
D_0\{n\operatorname{BR}_{\Pi_n}(r)-1\}\ge{}&
\Delta-j_nH-4u-8\alpha W-128\alpha^3\Gamma L^2\\
&-32\alpha^2\Gamma^2(1+u)-8\alpha^2\Gamma^2j_nH.
\end{split}
\tag{31}
\]
For clarity, the leading terms in this expansion are
\[
H(1-s)^2-D_0+D_0\left(\mathbb E\sigma^2-\sum_aq_a\mathbb E(C_a^2/V_a)\right),
\]
where (29) writes \(s=4\mathbb E\sigma^2/H+e\), \(|He|\le64\alpha^3\Gamma L^2\); the bounds \(D_0-8\ge-8\), \(1+u\le2\), and (16) give exactly the conservative constants in (31).

The following three finite tests imply that the right side of (31) is nonnegative:
\[
8\alpha^2\Gamma^2\le1,\qquad
j_n(1+4/\Delta_0)\le1/4,
\tag{32}
\]
\[
4u+8\alpha W+128\alpha^3\Gamma L^2
+32\alpha^2\Gamma^2(1+u)\le\Delta_0/2.
\tag{33}
\]
Indeed, \(H=4+\Delta\le\Delta(1+4/\Delta_0)\); (32) bounds the two \(j_nH\) terms together by \(\Delta/2\), and (33) bounds the remaining terms by \(\Delta/2\).  All tests eventually hold: after division by \(\Delta_0=4n^{-1/4}\), the slowest term is \(\alpha/\Delta_0=n^{-1/12}\).  Hence every positive exterior allocation satisfies
\[
\operatorname{BR}_{\Pi_n}(r)\ge1/n.
\tag{34}
\]

Finally, suppose an active arm \(a\) has \(q_a=0\).  Take \(z=e_a/c_a\) and write \(B^{-1}z=(1,\beta)\).  Every observed active marginal then has directional derivative zero, so the likelihood contribution in (21) is exactly zero; (20) has numerator \(\alpha\).  The same finite coordinate bound as in (28) gives \(J_D\le J_{\max}\).  Therefore
\[
\operatorname{BR}_{\Pi_n}(r)\ge\alpha^2/J_{\max}\ge1/n
\tag{35}
\]
once \(\alpha J_{\max}\le1\).  This includes allocations supported entirely on inactive arms.

Equations (25), (34), and (35) cover every count vector.  To obtain the sharp coefficient with an \(o(n^{-4/3})\) remainder, choose a sequence \(f_m\) for which the left side of (13) decreases to \(\Lambda_c\), choose \(\varepsilon_m\downarrow0\) so that \(\varepsilon_m\sum_jk_j\to0\), and for each fixed \(m\) choose a threshold \(N_m\) beyond which (11), (26), and (32)--(35) hold with error at most \(1/m\).  Taking \(m=m(n)\uparrow\infty\) sufficiently slowly and using the corresponding tube at sample size \(n\) proves
\[
\inf_r\operatorname{BR}_{\Pi_n}(r)
\ge n^{-1}-\Lambda_cn^{-4/3}-o(n^{-4/3}).
\]

For a possibly dependent outcome-independent design, \(Z\) is independent of the prior schedule.  Conditional on each labeled \(Z=z\), permutation invariance makes the Bayes risk depend only on its count vector, and randomized estimators cannot beat the posterior mean under squared loss.  Averaging the last display with respect to any law of \(Z\) preserves it.  This completes the uniform all-design and all-estimator assertion.
body.justification: The full-dimensional response tube supplies the design-uniform Bayes witness at the sharp coefficient.
body.gap: The proof closes the exact-target weak-integration and all-allocation-face obstruction that is absent from the scalar two-arm reduction.
body.consumer: The universal lower theorem averages this countwise inequality over every dependent outcome-independent assignment law.
